item.title: Marlins outfielders collide, knock fly ball over wall to give Braves star a home run in brutal mishap
item.description: Two Miami Marlins outfielders colliding on the warning track, accidentally knocking Ronald Acuña Jr.'s deep fly ball over the wall for a homer.
item.content:encoded:
The Miami Marlins outfielders took the definition of outfield assist to a whole new level.

Normally, an outfield assist is credited to an outfielder when they throw a ball into the infield to record an out against a baserunner. In the bottom of the third inning of the Marlins’ 11-3 loss to the Atlanta Braves on Thursday at Truist Park, they did the complete opposite of recording an outfield assist.

With a man on first base, Braves star outfielder Ronald Acuña Jr. hammered Marlins' starter Janson Junk’s 79-mph sweeper to deep left-center field but didn’t quite get enough of it to clear the wall.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Luckily for Acuña, Marlins left fielder Heriberto Hernández and center fielder Esteury Ruiz did not communicate about who was going to catch the deep fly ball, and they collided with each other on the warning track. When Ruiz and Hernandez collided, the ball popped up and over the wall for a home run.

The two outfielders looked around on the ground for the ball only to realize they had knocked it over the wall.

Acuña stood on first base for a couple of seconds, unsure if it was a home run before he eventually rounded the bases. Ruiz said the two outfielders couldn’t hear each other.

"When I saw the ball, I thought it was leaving the ballpark," Ruiz said through an interpreter, per MLB.com. "While I was running, I noticed it was going to stay on the field. I said, 'I got it,' and you can see in the video that (Hernández) also said, 'I got it.' But we couldn't hear each other with the noise of the ballpark. We couldn't hear each other."

For Acuña, it was the first of two home runs he hit in the win. He hit his second home run over the right-field wall, with no help from the outfielders, in the eighth inning to give the Braves a 9-2 lead.

"The second one was special, because the first one told me I needed help," Acuña said, according to MLB.com.

"(Acuña) had a little angel on his shoulder tonight, or something," Braves first baseman Matt Olson said, according to MLB.com.

The Braves’ victory was their season-high eighth straight, as they continue to build on their 8 1/2 game lead in the National League East.

The Braves (70-45) will look to extend their winning streak against the New York Yankees (64-51) on Friday at 7:05 p.m. ET.

The Marlins (58-58) will look to bounce back against the Los Angeles Angels (56-59) on Friday at 7:10 p.m. ET.

item.title: Left-leaning comedian labeled 'childish' by conservative Jeff Dye after insult scrawled on Tesla
item.description: Jeff Dye posted Tesla security camera photos showing Laura Kightlinger writing "douche" on his windshield, calling it "inappropriate for a 60-year-old."
item.content:encoded:
Comedian Jeff Dye fired back after catching fellow performer Laura Kightlinger scrawling an insult across his Tesla, blasting her conduct as "inappropriate for a 60-year-old" woman.

Dye took to X Monday, where he posted snapshots from video he said was captured by his Tesla’s security cameras showing a fellow comedian he’d performed with writing an insult in the fog on his windshield.

"Performed on a show with a comic I’ve never met. Her name is Laura Kightlinger @KingKightlinger. She seemed nice enough. We didn’t talk and she left before I went up," Dye wrote, adding, "I’m assuming she didn’t know it was my Tesla she wrote ‘Douche’ on my Tesla. Strange behavior for a 60-year-old adult. Look forward to working with you again."

ROGAN TELLS ‘TRAITOR’ COMEDIANS CONDEMNING THE KEVIN HART ROAST TO ‘F--- ALL THE WAY OFF’

The photos gained traction online, with over 440,000 views. Dye posted a follow-up noting that if he’d written something similar on her car, she would’ve spent the next 3 weeks talking about how ‘women are treated differently in Comedy,’ and how even in her own business she ‘doesn’t feel safe.’"

Kightlinger is a writer and comedian, known for serving as a consulting producer on "Will & Grace" and for having several half-hour specials on Comedy Central and HBO. She appeared to endorse Senator Bernie Sanders for President in the 2016 U.S. presidential election.

Dye is an outspoken conservative, and told Fox News Digital in December that he’s "always been more conservative than my comedic counterparts. I've always been way more religious as far as like, I'm a Christian, so that's not a huge, popular thing in stand-up comedy. I was on the front lines in that way."

Following Dye’s post on X, Kightlinger posted her side of the story and a photo of the word she wrote on the windshield alongside screenshots of messages she’d since sent Dye.

CONAN O'BRIEN, ZACH GALIFIANAKIS SAY IT'S A 'MISCONCEPTION' THAT COMEDY SHOWS ONLY TARGET CONSERVATIVES

"I was so annoyed by his taking down of a comic who had just performed I impulsively wrote douche in the fog on his car. The way you’re crying out about it should be embarrassing to tough-guy misogynists everywhere," Kightlinger responded.

The screenshots reveal she also apologized on social media, calling the decision "impulsive" and noting she should’ve brought her concerns to Dye directly. The messages show Dye arguing the comedian he’d spoken about "can take a joke," and calling Kightlinger’s actions "childish behavior."

KELSEY GRAMMER SUSPECTS HE 'MAY HAVE' LOST HOLLYWOOD ROLES DUE TO CONSERVATIVE VIEWS

He also directly responded to her on X again, adding, "Im not ‘Crying out’. Im simply holding you accountable for your bulls---. I’m also not a tough guy or a misogynist. I’m simply a fellow comedian that didn’t appreciate being called a name. I’d thought you’d understand that."

When reached for comment, Dye’s management gave Fox News Digital a statement from the comedian, noting his car was not vandalized other than the writing in the fog: "My car was not vandalized and my only motivation in posting the video online was to hold Laura Kightlinger accountable for being an a------."

"Writing insults on people’s property is a totally expected behavior for fatherless teens but inappropriate for 60 year old women," Dye added in the statement.

Entertainment reporter and host of the "Hollywood in Toto" podcast, Christian Toto, echoed that sentiment. He told Fox News Digital that the back-and-forth highlights partisan friction in the industry.

"Comedians in recent years, it's almost like they're picking sides in a way," Toto said, later adding that conservative comedians are often used to the criticism.

"When you're a right-leaning comedian, you expect some blowback. So it's not exactly unique territory for him," he said of Dye.

Toto added that while sharp elbows and teasing are standard protocol among comics, in some ways this incident broke traditional boundaries.

"If you're a comedian, you've got all the tools to fire back on stage, on social media or even in person," Toto said, later comparing that kind of exchange to "trash talking on the NBA court."

"The fact that she chose a different path, I don't think that suits her well," he added.

Fox News Digital also reached out to Kightlinger’s team for comment, but did not immediately hear back.

item.title: Jose Altuve's dominant history against Robbie Ray makes him a top player prop in Padres vs Astros
item.description: Robbie Ray makes his San Diego Padres debut against the Houston Astros, bringing Cy Young-caliber pitching and a 3.08 ERA to a crucial home matchup.
item.content:encoded:
We had the first football game of the season yesterday. Okay, so not really the actual season, but it was the official first preseason game of the NFL year, and we now have something like 20 straight weeks of football on Thursday nights from here on out. I don't know about you, but I can't wait. This has been a good baseball season, but football is still the king of sports. In order to build up our bankroll for the season, we should get some cash on this Astros and Padres game.

The Houston Astros are 59-57 for the season and currently sitting in first place in the AL West. It makes almost no sense to me that Houston would be in this position. I'm not surprised they are roughly a .500 team. Based on their roster, and their pitching especially, that checks out. What is surprising is that the Mariners (or even the Rangers) haven't taken over the division from them. The Astros still have the American League MVP, and maybe that's all they need in order to get the division this year.

I mentioned there have been issues with their pitching staff, and they even traded away a couple of guys before the trade deadline. I don't really think they took back any starter of substance, though. Today, for example, they are starting Ronel Blanco, who has only pitched in 14.2 innings this season. In the three games that he has pitched, he has given up at least three earned runs, walked at least two hitters, and allowed at least one homer. The most he pitched in any game was 5.1 innings. Padres hitters haven't seen Blanco much, with only three players ever facing him, and they are a combined 0-for-9.

The San Diego Padres are once again a disappointment. Did that prevent me from betting on them to win the World Series? Absolutely not. I generally think that talent wins out, and the Padres do have talent. The Dodgers have more talent than anyone, but the Padres' roster stacks up fairly well, even if their team is underperforming once again. Their best hitters are struggling this season, but if they can all lock in, San Diego can go on a tear like Boston has this season.

For whatever reason, it just never all seems to click at the right time for the Padres. Maybe I just overvalue their players for some reason. They once again went out and added to their team in hopes of making the push for the World Series. They traded for Robbie Ray, who starts tonight. Ray comes to them with a 10-6 record, 3.08 ERA, and a 1.29 WHIP. At his best, Ray is Cy Young-caliber. At his worst, he is still a really strong and reliable pitcher. He is coming off of two fantastic months of work, allowing just 11 runs in his past 60 innings. The Astros have been good against Ray in the past, owning a 17-for-54 history.

The majority of the damage from the Astros has come from Jose Altuve. It probably makes sense to put a player prop on him to get 2+ total bases against Ray. He is 11-for-20 against him with six extra-base hits. Even better, Altuve has only struck out once against him, so he is putting the ball in play when he faces Ray.

In addition to the player prop, I will take the Padres to win this game. Ray has been locked in, and I really don't think the Astros are that good of a team. If you can count on the Padres anywhere, it is certainly at home they are 32-25 in San Diego for the season. Give me the Padres to win this one at -126.

item.title: DAVID MARCUS: Why rising prices may not cost Republicans as much as you think
item.description: The viral burrito debate reveals how Gen Z voters feel about affordability, and why Republicans think prices won't decide the 2026 midterms.
item.content:encoded:
The great burrito debate burst onto the social media scene this week after Turning Point USA's Andrew Kolvet posted that the Gen Z voters at his events are upset that the Mexican wraps cost $20 these days.

Reaction was swift, heated and mixed, with some commenters saying this proved prices and affordability are a major red flag for the GOP in the midterms. But others scolded the youths, claiming that "in their day," they survived five years on nothing but ramen noodles, peanut butter and the kindness of strangers.

The fairly obvious subtext to this debate is the war in Iran, as team "cheap burritos" insists the war must end now to bring down prices and win in November, and team "suck it up, kids" argues that long-term economic success requires winning the war.

REPUBLICANS FACE TICKING MIDTERM CLOCK AS IRAN FALLOUT KEEPS PRESSURE ON GAS PRICES

The real question, for Republicans and the Trump administration, is just how angry are Americans over prices, and will that anger make them choose Democrats over the status quo?

To answer this question, it is important to understand that there are two kinds of political issues: gut and mental. Crime, for example, is a gut issue, because if you don’t feel safe on the street you feel it in your gut. Foreign policy, on the other hand, for most Americans, is a mental issue in that you think about it more than you feel it.

Affordability and prices can be a gut issue, and have been in several recent elections. If you are in line at the grocery store watching the tally rack up and hoping you have enough money for it, that is something you feel in the pit of your stomach.

In the fall of 2024, I was in Bedford, Pa., talking to some voters when a woman walked into the restaurant and, apropos of nothing, announced, "I cannot believe how much I just paid for groceries," to nods and grunts of angry assent.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS WANT MAJOR CHANGE AMID ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL DISCONTENT

This was not an uncommon occurrence two years ago. Cost of living and prices were not just the top issue for most voters I spoke with, but in many cases it all but eclipsed any others because they really were feeling it. You could see it in their eyes.

In Detroit last month, voters I spoke to were not obsessed with prices. In fact, most felt that Motown was seeing a revival, which helps to explain why, despite a very narrow statewide primary victory for Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, he lost the city badly to the more mainstream, less economically populist Rep. Haley Stevens.

This spring, there was a three-week-or-so period when gas prices really rocketed, and it became the complaint on everyone’s tongue. It was becoming a gut issue, but then the prices eased, and since have stayed in the "I don’t love it, but I can live with it" range.

As for the young adult Gen Z voters feeling an economic pinch, they have some real complaints, even if overpriced Door-Dash meals are not chief among them. The fact is that the cost of entry into adulthood is much higher than it was 30 years ago.

DEMOCRATS LURE ‘POLITICALLY HOMELESS’ GEN Z TOWARD SOCIALISM — A COUNTERATTACK IS TAKING SHAPE

When my then-girlfriend and I moved in together in 1995, we had to pay for rent, a landline (which cost almost nothing), and a couple of utility bills. There was no internet or cell phone bill, and our only subscription was to the journal Lingua Franca.

Republicans should be able to appeal to many of these frustrated young voters with targeted economic relief, something the Trump tax cuts achieved, for example, instead of the snake oil of socialism that the newfangled Democratic Party of Hasan Piker is hawking to them.

Everybody remembers the folly of President Joe Biden telling Americans that they didn’t know how good they had it while they were tightening their belts, and part of that was that Grandpa Joe was trying to talk intellectually about what had become a gut issue.

As far as Iran goes, the only theater of this particular war that the American people really care about is the gas station. If Trump can keep prices moderate, he can lob the occasional bomb at the mullahs until the cows come home.

100 DAY SPRINT TO THE MIDTERMS KICKS OFF AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS CLASH FOR CONTROL ACROSS THE COUNTRY

The 2026 election is becoming a stark choice between Republicans promising slow and steady progress and Democrats who want to blow up the system and start over, without a Senate, with a packed Supreme Court and with no private health insurance.

Unless something catastrophic happens between now and November, that is a choice that benefits the GOP, and it's why prices will not be as decisive as so many believe they will be.

item.title: Cambridge University professor resigns after major plagiarism accusations prompt investigation
item.description: Sociology professor Jason Arday resigned on Wednesday after triggering a Cambridge University investigation following several plagiarism accusations.
item.content:encoded:
University of Cambridge sociology professor Jason Arday resigned Wednesday after the university announced an investigation into his academic qualifications and honorary appointments amid plagiarism accusations, with one accuser telling Fox that Arday had been hired to be the "face of DEI."

Accusations against Arday surfaced last month from former Cambridge philosophy researcher Nathan Cofnas, who published a Substack article alleging that Arday was a known "plagiarist and fabulist" for more than a year, and much of his personal biography was questionable.

"I am disappointed that Jason Arday resigned. He was hired by Cambridge to be the face of DEI, and he was doing a great job," Cofnas told Fox News Digital.

Cofnas first expressed doubt about Arday's background after the educator said he had been nonverbal until age eleven and practically illiterate until 18 while still being able to get a Ph.D in 2015 and become the youngest Black professor at Cambridge University in 2023.

NEW YORK MAGAZINE COLUMNIST ACCUSED OF PLAGIARISM BY FELLOW REPORTERS, TRIGGERS INTERNAL REVIEW

Using the plagiarism-detection program, Copyleaks, Cofnas said he found several examples of Arday directly lifting materials from a 2009 dissertation without proper citation and sometimes even retaining copy-editing mistakes. Other earlier papers written by Arday were also issued corrections to add more citations, which Cofnas characterized as an admission of plagiarism.

From his research, Cofnas accused the university of hiring Arday to push diversity politics and has since been attempting to cover up plagiarism accusations to protect him from scrutiny.

"When you take away the work that is plagiarized or not otherwise written by Arday, there is essentially nothing resembling real scholarship," Cofnas wrote. "There is no indication that Arday is familiar with even elementary statistics. His research involves reporting his own experiences of alleged racism or having conversations with people and providing subjective commentary."

Arday's appointment in 2023 received massive media attention, with much of it celebrating it as a landmark moment.

Other media outlets and academics began reporting on the accusations, however, such as the Telegraph, the Guardian and the Times of London. Cambridge University initially stood by Arday in a statement on Sunday, saying Arday had already been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University and other journals for plagiarism. However, by Wednesday, Cambridge announced it was reversing course.

HARVARD CHIEF DEI OFFICER ACCUSED OF 40 COUNTS OF PLAGIARISM, INCLUDING LIFTING FROM HER OWN HUSBAND: REPORT

"The University of Cambridge has begun an investigation following new information about Professor Arday’s academic qualifications and honorary appointments. In order to ensure a fair process, we will not comment further until this has concluded," the statement read.

Shortly after the statement was released, Arday released his own statement through the Good Law Project announcing that he was resigning with "immediate effect," noting "public scrutiny" as a factor.

"Sadly, the years since my appointment have also been marked by an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack. While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement. The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love," Arday wrote.

HARVARD ATTEMPTING TO ‘REDEFINE’ PLAGIARISM TO PROTECT EMBATTLED PRESIDENT CLAUDINE GAY, ALLEGED VICTIM SAYS

He continued, "I have tried to continue because I believe deeply in the values of higher education, in rigorous scholarship, and in the transformative power of universities. I have tried because of my students, my colleagues and the countless people who have written to tell me that my journey gave them hope. But there comes a point when the personal cost becomes too great."

Fox News Digital reached out to Cambridge University and Arday for comment.

Cofnas added to Fox News Digital, "However, given that he is gone, a number of people have suggested that his professorship should be given to me. If the Cambridge administration could arrange this, it would go a long way toward restoring trust in higher education."

Cofnas was ousted from Cambridge in 2024 amid criticism of his writing that Blacks would almost completely "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment" in a world of full meritocracy.

item.title: Vehicle narrowly avoids slamming into driver on side of Ohio highway, dramatic video shows
item.description: Video from the Ohio Department of Transportation captures the moment a driver leaps onto a highway divider seconds before a sedan slams into his SUV.
item.content:encoded:
A vehicle narrowly avoided slamming into a driver on the side of an Ohio highway Monday, video released by the state Department of Transportation shows.

The motorist was standing along Columbus' I-670 adjacent to his vehicle, which was parallel to the road after seemingly striking the highway divider.

Video then shows a sedan careening toward the driver and his vehicle. The man, noticing the oncoming vehicle, hoists himself onto the highway median at the last second. The oncoming vehicle then smashes into his SUV, the footage shows.

According to a 911 call obtained by local news outlet ABC6, the SUV had a passenger in it at the time of impact.

The passenger told 911 operators that their vehicle had lost a tire and hit the highway divider before the crash.

"It’s off to the side but we are right in the turnstile, and it's really worrying me because we’re going to get hit," the passenger told operators, according to ABC6.

Fox News Digital contacted the Ohio Department of Transportation for updates on the conditions of the passengers involved.

TRUMP TAPS VETERANS TO FIX ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKING PROBLEM PLAGUING US ROADWAYS

A department spokesman highlighted the incident as a safety lesson, noting that the lane the impacted vehicle was in was closed and should not have had any other cars driving in it.

"There will be a green arrow over it if it's opened, a red X if it is closed. In this case, it was an emergency shoulder, so the person who crashed was stopped on the shoulder of the highway. They were doing the right thing. There should be nobody driving in that lane," Ohio Department of Transportation press secretary Matt Bruning told reporters.

The emergency lane, Bruning explained to Fox News Digital, was a "SmartLane," a highway feature in Ohio that allows the state to convert the wide shoulder into a temporary travel lane as needed. The SmartLane was closed at the time of the crash.

"Don't drive in a closed lane. If you are going to drive on the highway, allow that extra space between you and the vehicle in front of you so you have time to react and space to react if something might happen," Bruning concluded.

item.title: Ex-Obama, Biden diplomat blasts former boss’ border failures: 'They woke up too late'
item.description: Ken Salazar says the Biden administration "woke up too late" on the border crisis, creating a vacuum that handed Trump his strongest political issue.
item.content:encoded:
Former Cabinet secretary and U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ken Salazar says the Biden administration "woke up too late" to address the border crisis, arguing its failure to prioritize Mexico and effectively communicate its strategy helped hand President Donald Trump one of his strongest political issues.

Salazar, whose family has lived in the southwest since it was part of Mexico, laid out in his new book "Borderlands" how America’s foreign policy is too often on an "east-west paradigm" looking to Asia and Europe and neglecting Mexico and the Americas. He also argued that same mindset plagued the Biden administration, leaving it overly focused on Europe and Asia while neglecting Mexico and the Western Hemisphere.

"From day one, there should have been a great sense of urgency in addressing the crisis of a broken border and the migration crisis that we are seeing," Salazar said, arguing the Biden White House lacked both a comprehensive strategy and a coherent communications operation, creating what he described as a communications vacuum that Republicans filled.

BOMBSHELL MEMO SHOWS BIDEN PLANNED TO LEAVE TRUMP WITH EVEN MORE MASSIVE IMMIGRATION CRISIS

"I think that's what trapped the administration into this sense that they woke up too late by the time they did the right things to get control of the border," he said.

In the book, he recounts nearly resigning from his ambassadorship during a visit to Mexico with Biden and several inner-circle officials after being left out of an important meeting where he wanted to make the case for appointing a border-and-migration czar.

After one meeting at the Palacio Nacional in Mexico City, Salazar wrote that he decided to present his plan the next day but found out that he and former Sen. Christopher Dodd, D-Conn., weren’t going to be in the key meeting the next day.

Ultimately, he was able to meet privately with Biden at the last minute, where he expressed his concerns:

"We need someone in the White House to oversee the border, migration, Mexico, and the Americas. No one is in charge now. We need a border and migration czar," he said, reminding Biden that adviser Jeffrey Zients served as a "czar" for the COVID-19 response.

"[We need] someone focused exclusively on this crisis, with the authority to coordinate and direct action across agencies in Washington and communicate the message with one voice on these issues. With all due respect, Mr. President, if we are to succeed, it is urgent that we have someone like this in charge."

Salazar wrote that even after Biden's June 2024 executive order sharply reduced crossings, the administration failed to communicate the policy's success before Biden exited the race.

He said that gave President Donald Trump an opportunity to campaign on the "low-hanging fruit" of the border crisis.

TANVI RATNA: LATIN AMERICA'S RIGHT TURN IS REDRAWING THE UNITED STATES' BACKYARD

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and Biden for comment.

Both Biden and Trump, however, displayed what Salazar called "foreign policy malpractice" in terms of the Americas — something administrations have struggled with for 100 years, according to Salazar.

"That’s where everybody gets trapped," he said.

"Republicans, like Donald Trump, use it as a political advantage because that's how they win elections. And they realized that way back 20-some years ago."

"Democrats, on the other hand, have a sense that it is very important. And they do focus, but only on the border and on domestic migration issues [like] immigration reform. They don't focus at all or enough on Mexico [or] the border between Mexico and Guatemala — And that's what I believe we have to do. And that is what 'Borderlands' proposes that we do," he said, referring to his book.

HARRIS CALLS FOR ICE PROBE AFTER MAINE SHOOTING AMID RENEWED 'BORDER CZAR' CRITICISM

TRUMP BORDER CZAR TOM HOMAN WANTS POPE LEO XIV TO RIDE ALONG WITH ICE AGENTS: 'THEY DON'T UNDERSTAND'

Instead of demonizing migrants or focusing only on social aspects of the crisis, Salazar said his "Borderlands Platform" is a new vision that is grounded in realizing economic and national security prosperity for all three North American countries.

Salazar's proposed "Borderlands Platform" calls for a "New American Alliance" among the United States, Mexico and Canada, including deeper security cooperation, expanded labor mobility and renewed investment in North American trade. He argued immigration policy should be treated as both a national security and economic issue rather than solely a domestic political fight — and wrote supportively about renewing Trump’s USMCA, which had supplanted Bill Clinton’s NAFTA.

Salazar said Trump is correct that the border is "broken," but said he disagreed with Trump's approach, calling it divisive and pointing to ICE-involved shootings.

"It's not the American way where people have rights, where you have a sense of security, understand the importance of our security within our own country and the importance for supporting law enforcement."

Salazar pointed to his tenure as Colorado attorney general, where he led "thousands of cops," as evidence of his longstanding support for law enforcement.

KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY

"What is being neglected here is the bigger picture. And that's this foreign policy paradigm that is so required for the United States and Mexico and the Americas. And I don't see this administration moving in that direction to create the kind of legal frameworks that are essential that will give us our national security and ensure that we have a border that works and ensure we have an immigration system that is reformed and does the right thing," he said.

Salazar confirmed he has met with several Democrats viewed as potential 2028 presidential contenders, strongly advising them to make border and migration policy a top issue.

"Not that I have a lot of sway, but at least I will do everything I can to make sure that this is at the heart of every Democrat running for president," he said, noting that Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., was one lawmaker who met with him and endorsed his "Borderlands" book.

Asked if he would entertain Republican invitations, Salazar said if Trump reached out he would meet with him, but underlined that he would not become "political fodder for anybody."

TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED

"I do think that the Trump administration has an opportunity here because they, at the end of the day, recognize that the big questions of our time are affordability for the American people. The cost of strawberries, blueberries, and avocados, food, fuel, all those things are very much impacted by what's happening with tariffs and the uncertainty with Mexico right now," he said.

"I spent a lot of time on our ranch, I pumped the diesel into our [machinery], and I can tell you that across rural America, people are hurting because of what's happening with trade and we are losing a lot of our advantage here. Agriculture is in for a very hard time in the years ahead."

He said he hopes Trump would consider a "Borderlands"-type plan for a "new era" in Intracontinental relations.

"I don’t think that’s going to happen, but I certainly would give him that advice."

item.title: Pentagon plots new nuclear options for Trump as America’s biggest adversaries raise stakes: report
item.description: President Donald Trump could gain new tactical nuclear weapons options under a classified Pentagon strategy led by Elbridge Colby, NBC reports.
item.content:encoded:
The Pentagon is drafting a new nuclear strategy aimed at giving President Donald Trump more options for using shorter-range nuclear weapons in a potential regional conflict with China or Russia, according to a report.

The classified effort, led by Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby, would put greater emphasis on tactical nuclear weapons — systems intended for use against military targets in a regional conflict — rather than relying primarily on long-range strategic forces, NBC News reported, citing five people familiar with the plans.

The strategy is designed for scenarios in which China or Russia attacks a U.S. ally and Washington must determine how to respond without immediately escalating to a large-scale strategic nuclear exchange, according to the report.

TRUMP HEADS TO BEIJING FOR HIGH-STAKES XI TALKS AS TAIWAN TENSIONS, TRADE DISPUTES TEST US STRENGTH

"Our view is that we need credible nuclear options," a senior War Department official told NBC. The official said the strategy would "expand the President’s option space by providing him with realistic and credible options and therefore strengthen deterrence."

The reported shift comes as the United States confronts two nuclear-armed adversaries with increasingly capable arsenals.

Russia retains a large stockpile of theater nuclear weapons and has repeatedly invoked its nuclear capabilities during the war in Ukraine. China, meanwhile, is rapidly expanding and modernizing its nuclear forces, creating what U.S. military officials increasingly describe as a two-peer nuclear challenge.

Tactical, or non-strategic, nuclear weapons are generally designed for theater or regional use rather than long-range strategic missions. They often have shorter-range delivery systems and may be intended for military targets.

But the label does not mean they are limited in consequence: a nuclear detonation could kill large numbers of people, spread radioactive fallout and trigger nuclear retaliation.

US FALLS BEHIND IN HYPERSONIC RACE AS CHINA, RUSSIA GAIN EDGE

The War Department has not publicly announced a change in nuclear employment policy or a new tactical nuclear weapons program. Fox News Digital has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

The review also comes six months after New START, the last treaty limiting U.S. and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals, expired without a replacement, leaving Washington and Moscow without binding limits or inspections for the first time in decades.

The treaty did not cover tactical nuclear weapons, an area in which Russia holds a substantial numerical advantage. U.S. Strategic Command estimated this year that Moscow possesses up to 2,000 theater nuclear warheads.

Russia has long relied on its non-strategic nuclear arsenal in part to offset NATO’s conventional military strength. China’s growing arsenal is adding a separate challenge for Pentagon planners preparing for the possibility of confronting two nuclear-armed competitors.

Supporters of the Pentagon’s reported shift argue that giving Trump more credible limited-response options could strengthen deterrence by convincing an adversary that Washington has ways to respond short of an all-out strategic exchange.

Critics argue that putting greater emphasis on weapons intended for regional use could lower the threshold for nuclear employment and increase the risk that a limited conflict spirals into a broader nuclear war.

item.content:encoded:
Pete Crow-Armstrong angered a major baseball purist when he brought up a wild conspiracy theory that Babe Ruth did not exist.

"We always talk about how the game is evolving, and people may as well have been under handing the ball to that guy, and he's still regarded as one of the best players ever. You might as well dive further into it and be like, well maybe he just never existed."

That quote got the attention of longtime talking head and former MLB Network host Chris "Mad Dog" Russo, who said his "derogatory" comments on Ruth "drove me nuts."

"Hey Pete, you’re talking to me now about Ruth! Nobody hit home runs like Babe Ruth. Say what you want about [Shohei] Ohtani, we understand that he’s a unicorn. Babe Ruth is so good it’s mind boggling," Russo began on "First Take" this week. "Did you know, Peter Crow-Armstrong, that Babe Ruth hit 27 home runs over 500 feet? [Barry] Bonds? Never. Not one… Ruth owned baseball, nobody hit home runs like Ruth! He out-homered leagues!

"To sit there and say they were pitching underhand, well why didn’t anybody else hit the home runs hitting underhand? Outside of Gehrig, nobody hit home runs! It drives me crazy, especially in baseball, it drives me crazy when I hear today’s athletes and media guys who are 30 years old, who disparage the old-time guys."

WOMAN SUES YANKEES FOR $10 MILLION, CLAIMING ERRANT BAT INTO STANDS CAUSED SEVERE INJURIES

Ruth, assuming he existed, became Major League Baseball's all-time leader in home runs on July 18, 1921, with his 139th home run - he hit 575 more to retire with 714, a record that stood until Hank Aaron surpassed him in 1974.

In 1920, Babe Ruth's 54 home runs were more than the totals of seven of the eight MLB teams in existence at the time. He did the same in his 60-homer season in 1927.

Ruth is the all-time leader in slugging percentage (.690) and OPS (1.164), becoming one of the game's greatest hitters after posting Hall of Fame numbers on the mound. item.title: 'Melrose Place' star Andrew Shue says 70% believe the American Dream is 'dead or dying'
item.description: Andrew Shue claims 70% of Americans believe the American dream is dead or dying, driving him to launch The Forum bipartisan civic initiative.
item.content:encoded:
Former "Melrose Place" star Andrew Shue believes that the majority of Americans have lost faith in the promise that once defined the country.

During an interview with Fox News Digital, the 59-year-old actor, who founded the new bipartisan initiative The Forum, shared his grim assessment of the current mood of citizens in the United States, arguing that people across the economic and political spectrum are struggling.

JOHN ADAMS MADE A TERRIFYING PREDICTION. AMERICA IS CLOSE TO PROVING HIM CORRECT

"There's nobody in this country right now that thinks we're in a good place," Shue said. "You look around and you say, how do we feel about our kids? How do we fill it feel about our kid's future? What kind of anxiety level do we all have? You're seeing 70% believe the American dream is dead or dying."

"So we're all in this boat together," he continued. "There's nobody who's jumping out, whether you're a billionaire, a bartender, everybody in between, we are all in this together."

Shue said that Americans' growing pessimism is not being driven by a single election or political figure, but by systemic problems he believes have accumulated over decades.

"We're realizing that the engine is broken and the main systems that drive that engine are our political system and our economic system," Shue explained. "The political system only rewards people in power — there happen to be a lot of old people — and performative conflict. The economic system is really just rewarding people at the top. Ninety percent feel like they're treading water or underwater, and have been for decades. The other thing I'll say is all of these problems existed long before [current U.S. President] Donald Trump came to the scene."

WATCH HERE: ‘MELROSE PLACE’ ALUM ANDREW SHUE SAYS 70% BELIEVE THE AMERICAN DREAM IS ‘DEAD OR DYING’

WORLD SERIES CHAMPION JOE GIRARDI REVEALS WHAT HE FINDS MOST 'DISTURBING' ABOUT POLITICS TODAY

"And so, as we look around, and we're fighting each other, and we try to figure out, what are we gonna do? Who's coming to save us? The answer is right in front of us," he continued. "It's us. It's the American people. The question is, ‘Oh, that seems kind of obvious. Yeah, the consent of the governed.’ We are the ones who are supposed to be the ultimate authority."

To help address what he sees as the country's growing divide, Shue founded The Forum, a nonpartisan civic initiative that brings together politically diverse Americans to identify areas of agreement and develop policy proposals. The initiative has already been implemented in three early primary states, including South Carolina, New Hampshire and Nevada.

"We have launched the Forum that I've been working on for the last eight years with an incredible team," he said. "It's the place and the process for the American people to co-create that renewal agenda. Over 300,000 people have participated so far. Perfectly politically balanced — conservatives showing up, liberals showing up, people on the far left, far right — everybody's showing up, and we have credibility and legitimacy."

"Elected leaders from both sides who put down their arms are actually leading the efforts in each state," he added. "So this is the way forward. The question is, will the legislators, the elected leaders, follow? The American people are ready to lead."

SEN CHUCK SCHUMER UNVEILS ANTI-CORRUPTION AGENCY AIMED AT TRUMP AND FUTURE PRESIDENTS

As the initiative has expanded across three states, Shue told Fox News Digital that he has been struck by how quickly participants find common ground despite their political differences.

"I think that the thing that surprised me the most was that when you give people this assignment, you say, 'It's now on you, you are going to be the hero of the story. All you have to do is work together, listen to each other, listen to your lived experiences, and come up with something that you can agree on,'" Shue said.

WATCH HERE: ‘MELROSE PLACE’ ALUM ANDREW SHUE LAUNCHES NEW BIPARTISAN INITIATIVE THE FORUM TO BREAK AMERICA'S POLITICAL GRIDLOCK

"And 70% have to agree — that's the supermajority number, 70% or higher — and then it can go forward as draft legislation," he continued. "And the thing that's beautiful is when you get these people in the rooms with people who are different, they can't figure out who the Democrat or the Republican is. They see all the common values. They see the common goal."

"Once you start listening to each other, once you start feeling like you're on the same team, and you have the same goal, anything's possible," Shue added. "And people are desperate. That's the thing. People are desperate. They're really ready for something new."

AS AMERICA MARKS 250 YEARS, OUR GREATEST CHAPTERS ARE STILL AHEAD OF US

The Delaware native also reflected on what has restored his optimism about Americans and what they can achieve when they are united.

"That we know what makes America, America," he said. "It's about that confidence, that belief in what's possible. You know, I think [U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it best, 'Anyone from anywhere can become anything.' And people believe that and they live that."

item.title: READ THE DOCUMENTS: Secret ‘Oxferd Comma’ probe cast Trump as potential Russian asset after Comey firing
item.description: The FBI opened a counterintelligence probe codenamed "Oxferd Comma" after Trump fired James Comey, seeking direct ties to the Russian Federation.
item.content:encoded:
The White House released a trove of documents showing that the FBI opened a 2017 investigation into whether President Donald Trump was acting on behalf of or under the influence of Russia when he fired FBI Director James Comey.

The investigation, codenamed "Oxferd Comma," opened after Trump fired Comey in May 2017, according to the White House’s release. 

Investigators sought to determine whether Trump was "directed by, controlled by, and/or coordinated activities with, the Russian Federation in a manner constituting a threat to the national security of the United States and/or a violation of federal criminal statutes," according to an FBI memo dated May 16, 2017. The memo also said investigators would examine whether Trump or others had obstructed or conspired to obstruct an associated FBI investigation.

TRUMP ALLY DIGENOVA TAPPED TO LEAD DOJ PROBE INTO BRENNAN OVER RUSSIA PROBE ORIGINS

The opening memo cited information developed during Crossfire Hurricane, the FBI’s counterintelligence investigation into whether individuals associated with Trump’s 2016 campaign were coordinating with the Russian government to interfere in the 2016 election.

READ THE DOCUMENTS:

It also identified later events and information, including Trump’s interactions with Comey, the administration’s shifting explanations for Comey’s firing, Trump campaign discussions concerning the Republican platform’s language on Ukraine aid and Trump’s business ties and real estate interests involving Russia.

SECRET FBI PROBE CAST TRUMP AS POSSIBLE RUSSIAN ASSET AFTER COMEY FIRING, MEMOS SHOW

Trump initially cited Comey’s handling of the FBI investigation into Hillary Clinton’s use of a private email server while she was secretary of state as the reason for his ouster, though he later said the Russia investigation was also on his mind when he made the decision.

The FBI memo said the circumstances surrounding Comey’s dismissal could support an inference that the bureau’s counterintelligence investigation was a factor in Trump’s decision to fire Comey.

READ THE DOCUMENTS:

However, the decision to open the investigation did not mean those suspicions had been substantiated.

Special counsel Robert Mueller, appointed in 2017 to investigate Russian election interference, reported in 2019 that his team did not establish coordination between the Trump campaign and Russia and did not make a prosecutorial decision on obstruction. Attorney General William Barr appointed John Durham to review the origins and handling of the FBI’s Russia investigation in 2019. Durham’s 2023 report concluded that the FBI opened the full Crossfire Hurricane investigation without sufficient evidentiary support and did not apply the same rigor it had used in other sensitive investigations.

READ THE DOCUMENTS:

A separate 2019 Justice Department inspector general review found the FBI had enough information under its rules to open Crossfire Hurricane, though it later identified serious errors and omissions in surveillance applications involving former Trump campaign adviser Carter Page.

A review of the White House’s original release shows the code name rendered as "Oxferd Comma," with the letter "o." Former acting Assistant Attorney General Jeff Clark, who served in Trump’s first administration, said a document expert he consulted concluded the "o" in "Comma" found within the FBI documents was a zero. Clark speculated the unusual spelling was intended to make the records harder to find through FOIA searches.

The documents were published by the White House Wednesday, which said they had been declassified and released through its Government Transparency Task Force.

item.title: Senate Republicans push Election Day deadline for California's marathon ballot counts
item.description: Sens. James Lankford and Mike Lee cite a Supreme Court ruling as they push legislation requiring all mail-in ballots be received by the time polls close.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: A pair of Senate Republicans are bursting through a crack in the door left by the Supreme Court to force blue states like California to vastly cut down on how long it takes to count ballots.

Sens. James Lankford, R-Okla., and Mike Lee, R-Utah, are introducing legislation that would create a federal deadline for states to accept ballots received by the time polls close on Election Day across the country.

Lankford pitched the bill, called the Ballots by Election Day Act, as a bid to build more trust in the country’s elections.

TRUMP UNLOADS AFTER SUPREME COURT UPHOLDS LATE MAIL-IN BALLOTS IN MISSISSIPPI

"I have made fun of other states for years because there's quite a few states around the country that can't seem to figure out how to be able to count," Lankford told Fox News Digital in an interview. "In Oklahoma, our election ends at 7 p.m. on a Tuesday night."

"Usually by 9 p.m., all of our thousands of precincts are all in and counted," he continued. "We start the verification process. We do an audit after that. We have great trust in our elections because we know. We all vote. But we get them all in on that."

Lankford and Lee’s bill would create a nationwide deadline for counting absentee and mail-in ballots, meaning that if those ballots aren’t in by the time polls close across the expanse of time zones in the nation, they won’t be counted.

CALIFORNIA’S SLUGGISH VOTE COUNTING RIPPED ACROSS THE POLITICAL SPECTRUM: 'EXTREMELY EMBARRASSING'

It targets states, like California and Washington state, where ballot counting can take days, sometimes weeks, beyond when polls close.

"States counting late ballots are inviting fraud and sowing doubt in their own election results," Lee told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Our bill will clarify protocol and restore trust by counting only ballots received before the polls close on Election Day."

Lankford contended that those states, "like California and others, New York," breed distrust in the system.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP'S ELECTION ORDER AS SAVE AMERICA ACT FIGHT INTENSIFIES

"When you vote you may not know for weeks to months what the final election count is," he said. "That shouldn't be in the United States of America."

Their push comes after the Supreme Court’s decision to allow mail-in ballots post-marked before Election Day to still be counted if they came in later.

While the court contended that mail-in balloting could continue, it didn’t explicitly address that there could be no deadline for when the ballots could be counted.

"Once the court made their ruling, as that came out, they left a clear door open to say this could be defined by the United States Congress," Lankford said. "So I said, let's step in and actually do that. Let us provide some real clarity for that. This shouldn't be controversial. This should just be something to build trust in our elections."

item.title: Iran is moving its tanks. Decades as a military planner taught me what that means
item.description: Iran's 92nd Armored Division reportedly moved T-72 tanks toward Abadan even as diplomacy over the Strait of Hormuz and nuclear program advances.
item.content:encoded:
During nearly five decades in uniform and as a Pentagon strategist, I served alongside armored and mechanized forces in South Korea, at Fort Riley and in divided Cold War Germany. While stationed along the Iron Curtain, I helped plan the defense against a Soviet armor-heavy assault through the Fulda Gap and across NATO's central front. Later, during the Iraq War, I observed firsthand how American armored formations were employed in combat.

One lesson stayed with me.

Military professionals rarely begin by asking what politicians are saying. They begin by asking what armies are doing.

TRUMP MAY CLAIM HE WON THE FIGHT WITH IRAN, BUT THERE’S A BIGGER WAR ALREADY UNDERWAY

Professional soldiers are trained to see what others overlook. Not necessarily because they possess better information, but because they ask different questions.

Politicians communicate through speeches. Diplomats communicate through negotiations. Armies reveal themselves through force posture. A brigade quietly changes location. Engineers strengthen defensive positions. Fuel and ammunition move forward. Reserve formations reposition. None of those actions guarantee war, but together they often reveal something more valuable than public statements: what commanders believe may happen next.

US EYES FIRST-EVER HYPERSONIC DARK EAGLE DEPLOYMENT AS IRAN PUSHES BEYOND STRIKE RANGE

Throughout my career, I learned that tanks rarely tell you who is about to attack. They tell you what commanders think is coming.

That is why recent reports deserve careful attention. Elements reportedly associated with Iran's 92nd Armored Division moved T-72 tanks toward the southern approaches near Abadan on August 1. If confirmed, the movement matters, not because it proves an American ground campaign is imminent, but because it may reveal what Iranian planners are preparing to confront.

Professional militaries do not reposition conventional formations casually. Armor consumes enormous amounts of fuel and logistical support. Commanders accept those costs only when the movement serves a real operational purpose.

Whether Tehran ultimately employs those forces is almost beside the point.

The more important question is this: What does Iran believe may come next?

WEAPONS STOCKPILE SHORTAGES IMPACTING MILITARY STRATEGY IN THE MIDEAST

This distinction reflects the difference between military intelligence and operational planning. Intelligence assesses capabilities and intentions. Planners then translate that into a harder question: What mission does the adversary appear to be preparing to execute?

Force posture often reveals expectations more clearly than official statements, because governments can disguise intentions more easily than they can disguise preparations.

Armies rarely announce what they expect. They quietly organize for it.

The reported movement deserves attention precisely because it involves the Artesh rather than the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Americans understandably focus on the IRGC. It oversees Iran's missiles, drones, proxy forces and the security of the Islamic regime. The Artesh serves another purpose entirely. It is Iran's conventional army, organized principally to defend Iranian territory against external attack.

Military organizations reposition forces for many reasons: dispersing vulnerable assets, conducting an exercise, strengthening deterrence, signaling political resolve, or preparing for a changing mission. The planner's task is to determine which explanation best fits the broader pattern of events.

WHO IS AHMAD VAHIDI? IRAN’S NEW IRGC CHIEF TIED TO GLOBAL ATTACKS AND ‘DEATH TO AMERICA’ IDEOLOGY

In this case, if accurate, the more plausible explanation is not an offensive against neighboring states, but preparation for a fight that evolves beyond today's exchange of missiles, drones and airstrikes into one over Iranian territory itself.

That observation should not be misunderstood. It does not predict an American invasion of Iran.

Professional militaries prepare for possibilities long before political leaders decide whether those possibilities become policy. Military planning is an exercise in managing uncertainty. Good commanders prepare for futures they hope never occur, because hope has never been a planning assumption.

History repeatedly demonstrates why force posture deserves careful study. During the Cold War, NATO intelligence officers watched Warsaw Pact armored deployments almost continuously. Tanks alone never revealed Soviet intentions. Supporting engineers, logistics, artillery, bridging equipment and reserve movements often proved far more revealing.

Experienced planners learned to read military behavior the way physicians read symptoms: not as isolated facts, but as evidence of a larger condition. The task was spotting convergence, not isolated movement.

TRUMP WARNS IRAN WILL BE HIT 'REALLY HARD' IF NUCLEAR NEGOTIATIONS COLLAPSE AGAIN

The same lesson emerged when Saddam Hussein invaded Iran in September 1980. Saddam mistook revolutionary turmoil and military disorganization for strategic weakness. He expected a rapid victory. Instead, Iran reorganized, mobilized and transformed what Baghdad expected would be a short campaign into an exhausting eight-year war. Saddam confused visible weakness with imminent collapse, a mistake strategists should not repeat when assessing Iran today.

Many observers now assume the war in Ukraine demonstrated that tanks are obsolete. It demonstrated something more nuanced. Tanks operating without infantry, engineers, electronic warfare, air defense and drones become exceptionally vulnerable.

Yet tanks remain indispensable because armies still require protected mobility, mobile firepower and the ability to seize and hold terrain. Technology has changed how tanks fight. It has not changed why armies still need them.

ARMY IDS 2 VICTIMS KILLED IN JORDAN AIR BASE ATTACK; TRUMP: IRAN WILL PAY 'MANY TIMES OVER'

Iranian doctrine reflects the same reality. Its armored formations are not meant to defeat American forces tank for tank. They can reinforce corridors, support infantry, protect critical sites and complicate any attempt to seize terrain or expand a ground presence. Integrated with difficult terrain, prepared positions, mines and air defense, even aging armor can delay, disrupt and raise the cost of escalation.

Ironically, these reported military preparations come as diplomacy appears to be gaining momentum. Oman-mediated contacts between the United States and Iran have reportedly made progress toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz while creating an opportunity for broader discussions over Iran's nuclear program.

To many civilians, those developments appear contradictory.

Professional soldiers see them differently.

Experienced planners expect governments to negotiate while armies continue preparing for the possibility that negotiations fail. That is not cynicism; it is prudence. Military organizations exist to preserve options for political leaders should diplomacy falter, not because they expect war, but because they cannot afford to be surprised by it.

IRAN WAR'S PRICE TAG HITS $80B — MORE THAN DOUBLE WHAT CONGRESS WAS TOLD

That reality now confronts President Donald Trump. Military pressure appears to have created genuine diplomatic leverage. His challenge is converting that pressure into verifiable results, freedom of navigation through Hormuz, enforceable constraints on Iran's nuclear program and greater regional stability, before demands expand into objectives airpower alone cannot deliver.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

History suggests the hardest strategic decision is not when to begin military operations, but when additional destruction stops producing proportionate political gain.

Throughout my Army career, I learned that armies tip their hand long before they fight, not through speeches or press conferences, but through logistics, doctrine, training and force posture. Tanks are simply one part of that larger language.

Iran's aging armored vehicles may never fire a shot in this conflict. In fact, the tanks themselves are almost incidental. What matters is what their reported movement suggests about how Tehran may be thinking.

A strategist's first responsibility is not merely to prepare for the next battle, but to recognize when an adversary's preparations create an opportunity to prevent it. Reading force posture correctly is not simply about predicting war. At its best, it gives statesmen the understanding necessary to preserve peace before military expectations harden into military necessity.

CISA says the Russian state-sponsored group Laundry Bear can compromise certain email accounts when someone simply opens or previews a malicious message. The attack targets organizations running unpatched versions of the Zimbra Collaboration Suite.

Once the email appears, hidden code can collect passwords, authentication data and as much as 90 days of messages. You may never see a warning or realize that anything happened.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued the warning with the National Security Agency, FBI and cyber authorities from several allied countries. The agencies say the group has successfully targeted more than 10 Western organizations since July 2025.

Laundry Bear, which Microsoft tracks as Void Blizzard, exploits a security flaw known as CVE-2025-66376. The cross-site scripting vulnerability affects the Classic user interface in certain versions of the Zimbra Collaboration Suite.

Zimbra is an email and collaboration platform used by some governments, schools, businesses and other organizations as an alternative to services such as Microsoft Exchange or Google Workspace. Attackers can place malicious JavaScript inside a specially crafted HTML email. That code runs automatically when a vulnerable Zimbra webmail client displays the message.

The person reading the email does not need to open an attachment. The attack also avoids the usual request to enter a password on an obvious phishing page. However, the email still needs to appear on the screen. CISA describes the technique as a zero-click exploit. Proofpoint calls it a "half-click" attack because someone must open the email or allow it to appear in a preview pane. Either description leads to the same concern. A message can look harmless while code hidden inside it quietly attacks the email account.

Laundry Bear reportedly used the flaw as a zero-day before Zimbra released a patch in November 2025. A zero-day attack exploits a security weakness before the software maker provides a fix. CISA later added the vulnerability to its list of flaws that hackers actively exploit.

The available patch closes the known security hole. Yet Laundry Bear continues to target organizations that have not installed the update. That makes delayed patching especially dangerous. An organization may have strong passwords and trained employees, but an exposed email server can still give attackers another way inside.

The campaign has reached organizations connected to the defense industrial base and government. Attackers have also targeted education, energy, law enforcement, media, nonprofit groups and technology companies.

According to CISA, the malicious code attempts to collect the target's last 90 days of email. That could include private conversations with coworkers, contract discussions or information about upcoming meetings. An inbox may also contain password reset notices, invoices and documents that reveal how an organization operates.

Laundry Bear also collects the person's email address and password. The attack can copy the organization's Global Address List, which acts as a directory of employees and contacts. The hackers may then gain enough information to impersonate a trusted coworker or identify more valuable accounts.

CISA says the exploit also targets two-factor authentication tokens. Those tokens help prove that someone has already completed an authentication step. A stolen token or session cookie can let an attacker enter an account without completing the normal login process again.

FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK

Stealing information provides immediate value, but Laundry Bear also tries to preserve its access. The attack creates a new Zimbra application passcode and sends it back to the hackers. Legacy email programs use these passcodes when they connect through services such as IMAP or ActiveSync and cannot support modern time-based authentication.

An unauthorized passcode can give the hackers another entrance to the mailbox. That access may continue even after someone changes the main account password. CISA has urged administrators to look for suspicious application passcodes, particularly passcodes labeled "ZimbraWeb."

Organizations should treat an unknown passcode as a sign that someone may have entered the account. Simply installing the patch after a compromise may leave the attacker's access in place.

Laundry Bear sends the stolen information to servers controlled by the group. CISA says the attackers use a collection framework called Flowerbed. The system moves smaller pieces of data through Domain Name System requests. DNS normally helps computers find websites and online services.

Attackers can hide encoded information inside those requests. Because organizations generate large amounts of legitimate DNS traffic, the malicious activity may blend into the background. Laundry Bear sends larger collections through encrypted HTTPS connections. That can include compressed archives containing mailbox data. Security teams may need to inspect network logs, authentication records and mailbox activity to understand what left the organization.

Laundry Bear also uses adversary-in-the-middle phishing kits. These tools create login pages that closely resemble legitimate email portals. When someone enters a username and password, the phishing system captures those credentials. It can also intercept session cookies created during the login process. That means an attacker may gain access even when the account uses conventional multifactor authentication.

CISA's indicators of compromise include domains that impersonated Zimbra infrastructure. Examples include mailnalysis.com, zimbrastat.com, zimbra-metadata.com and zmailanalytics.com. The presence of one of these domains in network logs could point to phishing or unauthorized account activity. However, organizations should review CISA's complete list because attackers can change their infrastructure.

Proofpoint found that Laundry Bear sent messages from attacker-controlled Proton Mail accounts and email addresses the group had already compromised. In one example, the sender claimed to represent a Belgian media-verification organization. The email proposed cooperation between European institutions fighting disinformation. It included a legitimate-looking link to a European Union events calendar. However, the malicious code sat inside the email rather than the linked website.

Dutch intelligence agencies publicly identified Laundry Bear in May 2025. Their investigation linked the group to a 2024 breach of the Dutch National Police. That incident exposed personal information belonging to police personnel. Investigators said the attack helped them identify a previously unknown Russian cyberespionage group.

Since at least 2024, Laundry Bear has focused on organizations connected to Russian strategic interests. Its targets have included NATO member states and groups supporting Ukraine.

Microsoft has documented compromises involving defense organizations as well as entities in transportation and aviation.A separate campaign targeted members of Ukraine's military with charity-themed phishing emails. Those messages disguised malware as requests for donations.

These campaigns suggest the group cares more about long-term intelligence collection than a quick financial payout. Access to email can reveal relationships, future plans and internal decisions.

PAIDWORK BREACH EXPOSES 23M USER RECORDS

The strongest protection starts with the organization running the email server because employees cannot personally patch a vulnerable installation. However, you can still take steps to spot suspicious activity and protect your other accounts.

Administrators should update Zimbra Collaboration Suite to a currently supported version and install all available security fixes. Organizations should confirm that the patch reached every server. An overlooked system may remain exposed even when the primary mail server has received the update.

Installing the patch blocks the known flaw, but it cannot undo a previous intrusion. Security teams should review CISA's published indicators of compromise. They should also search network records for connections to the listed domains and IP addresses. Authentication logs may reveal unusual locations, unexpected devices or activity outside normal working hours.

Review every Zimbra application passcode connected to an account. Pay close attention to unfamiliar entries and anything labeled "ZimbraWeb." Revoke any passcode that the account owner or IT department cannot verify. Because application passcodes can survive a regular password change, this review plays an important role in removing persistent access.

Administrators should examine mailbox access records and forwarding settings. They should also look for unfamiliar filters, deleted messages or sent emails that the account owner does not recognize. A compromised account may send convincing phishing messages to coworkers because the email comes from a trusted internal address.

Contact your IT or security team if you notice unfamiliar sent messages, unexpected password resets or login alerts you cannot explain. Do not rely only on changing your password. Laundry Bear can create an application passcode that may continue providing mailbox access after the main password changes. Your IT team should revoke unauthorized passcodes, end active sessions and check the account for suspicious activity.

Wait until your IT department has patched the server and removed unauthorized access. Then change your email password and any other password you reused. Create a unique password for every account. A password manager can generate strong credentials and store them securely. Hackers may test stolen email credentials on banking, shopping or social media accounts. Reused passwords can turn one compromised inbox into several compromised accounts.

CISA recommends phishing-resistant multifactor authentication where organizations can support it. Security keys and passkeys provide stronger protection than methods that rely on temporary codes. However, organizations still need to patch the underlying email software. Authentication controls cannot fully protect an account when malicious code runs inside a vulnerable webmail interface.

Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious downloads, fake login pages and follow-up malware connected to a broader phishing campaign. However, antivirus software may not stop this email exploit because the malicious code runs inside a vulnerable webmail session. Your organization still needs to update Zimbra and investigate the account for unauthorized access. An email login page can look convincing and still belong to an attacker. Instead of following a link inside an email, open your organization's known webmail address directly. Report unfamiliar authentication requests or repeated sign-in prompts to your security team. A sudden request to log in again could signal a phishing attempt or unauthorized account activity.

For years, we have warned you to avoid suspicious links and unexpected attachments. That advice still helps, but Laundry Bear shows why your organization also needs to keep the software behind your inbox updated. In this campaign, viewing an email can trigger malicious code on an unpatched server. The attackers can then reach into the mailbox, collect months of messages and steal authentication data. The hidden application passcode adds another concern. Changing a password may provide a false sense of security when an attacker has already created a separate route back into the account. Organizations using Zimbra should patch immediately and then investigate for signs of earlier access. Employees should remain cautious around unexpected login pages, even when the page carries familiar company branding.
